---
name: choose
description: Build a decision page when the user has to choose. Use when a reply would otherwise ask the user to decide more than one thing, when a decision has more than two viable answers, when a list needs items marked for deletion, or when the user asks for a checklist to approve a batch of items one by one. Covers multiple choice, either or, free text, check box for deletion, and affirmative approval checklists. Triggers on help me choose, let me choose, give me options, give me choices, decision page, choice page, multiple choice, either or, checkbox for deletion, tick what to delete, which should I pick, ask me what I want, approve these constants, stamp these rules, approval checklist, and /choose.
user-invocable: true
argument-hint: "[what the decision is about]"
lifecycle:
  origin: "owner request 2026-08-20: four universal input shapes plus a reusable skill"
  class: build
  last_verified: "2026-08-20"
---

# Choose

A choice page collects decisions. It does not execute them. Build one only for a genuine
unresolved choice that belongs to the user: spend, credentials, live external mutations,
priorities, taste. Work the user already authorized as reversible gets no page; do the
work and report it with a one line revert. Match the interface to the task: ask a single
short question in the reply; use a working native choice control when the host supplies
one; build a page only when more than one decision is pending, one decision has more than
two viable answers, a list exists and some entries may need deleting, or the user
explicitly asked for an approval checklist over a batch of items.

## Register

<Every question, option, detail, and consequence on the page is written in the simple
register, `../simple/SKILL.md`: plain words a non-technical reader follows.> The page
addresses the reader as "you", never names the owner or refers to him in the third
person, carries no praise, and contains no writer's direction.

## Spec and builder

Read `references/spec-format.md` before writing a spec: every field, all question shapes,
the rejected prose list, the payload format, and a worked example. Build with the bundled
script, addressed relative to this skill's directory:

```bash
python3 scripts/build_choices.py --spec 'SPEC.json' --out 'TASK_OUTPUT/page.html'
```

Exit codes: 0 wrote, 2 invalid spec (every problem printed), 3 refused to overwrite an
existing `--out`, 4 template problem. A page never renders from a bad spec. Pass `--force`
only when the user asked to replace that exact file. Write the spec and page inside the
current task's output directory; do not select a global configuration directory as an output location. Replace TASK_OUTPUT with that directory. The output is one
self-contained HTML file (no network, fonts, CDN, or preview server) that opens whole
from disk by a click on the file, today or later.

## What cannot be skipped

- **Resolve governing constraints before you ask.** Read the applicable requirements,
  specs, and pinned tests before writing the answer space. Never present a prohibited
  option as shippable; state the conflict in that option's detail and recommend a
  compliant middle path when one exists.
- **Do the research before you ask.** If the answer space can be enumerated by looking it
  up, look it up and offer a `choice` with real numbers. "What budget do you approve"
  instead of pricing three vendors moves your work onto the user and costs a round trip.
- **Every question is answerable without a follow-up.** Read each one back as though you
  knew nothing else. If the honest reaction is "answer to what", rewrite it. The builder
  rejects the common forms and does not catch every one.
- **A quantity needs a unit.** Dollars per month, emails per day, days. The builder
  requires `unit` on any question using quantity language and refuses to build without it.
- **No hedging.** "Leave blank if you would rather" means the question is not settled.
  Settle it or drop it. This governs your prose, not the automatic free text box.
- **Never write your own "Other" option.** Every `choice`, `either`, `prune`, and `approve`
  question already renders a free text box ("Something else" or "Anything to add"); a
  `text` question is one already. Typed text answers a `choice` or `either` alone and
  deselects any card.
- **Every option carries the consequence, not just a label.** "Rotate the token" is a
  label. "Rotate the token, which restores the booking alert and takes about two minutes"
  is a choice the reader can make without a follow-up.
- **Mark the recommended option** wherever one exists, and put it first. A page with no
  recommendation hands the reader a blank page, which this skill exists to prevent.
- **A prune question starts with nothing ticked.** `suggest_delete` only adds a tag.
- **Approval is affirmative, never by default.** Anything the user ratifies uses the
  `approve` type: a tick is the yes, an unticked row is withheld, nothing is pre-ticked.
  Never model an approval as `prune`, whose untouched state reads as consent to everything.
  Owner ruling 2026-08-26, after a batch shipped as prune approved 12 rules with zero clicks.
- **State the before-state in any option that triggers a gated action.** The selection is
  the decision, and a decision without the before-state is not revertible.
- **Prefer fewer, sharper questions.** Each question costs attention; three answerable
  questions beat seven where two are vague.

## Approval checklists

When the user explicitly requests an approval checklist, build a one-question `approve`
page: one row per item, the label stating what ticking the row settles and carrying
the item's identifier, the item restated in plain words in the detail. The payload's `approved` array records what was ticked. A tick
records a proposed decision until the user submits it. Interpret submitted choices under the
current user authorization; do not ask again merely because a page collected the answer.
Where the operation requires mechanical authorization, use the existing bound mechanism.
Never claim that a tick, payload or paste redeems tokens through an absent component.

## Verification and handover

Verify the produced page, not the intent. With the native or browser tools available in
this session, open the built file and confirm: the build exited 0; every intended
question and option is present with its consequence and the recommended tag; one question
per screen; the prune and approve counters match what is ticked; typing in the free text
box on a `choice` deselects every card, satisfies the question alone, and reaches the
payload as `other`; the review screen jumps back on click; the copy button produces the
human summary followed by the JSON block; no horizontal overflow at 390px and 1440px.
If no tool in the session can open the page, state exactly which checks were not run. No
browser worker stage is required. A skill or script call by itself enforces nothing; a
Watch rule is enforced only where a working binding, observation, and validator exist.
<simple: the handover the user reads> Share the actual written path; if the host UI can
open or display a local file, use that route.

## Stopping and the free text override

A gated action still stops until the user's answer names it. If the user answers only part
of the page, act on what was answered and leave the rest pending. When a payload's `other`
note contradicts its `delete` ticks (2026-08-29, verbatim: "don't delete ones I checked
just tell me what they are in more detail"), the note wins: execute only the rows the note
leaves unambiguous, surface the ticked-but-contradicted rows as explanations or questions,
and never execute a deletion the user's own note told you to hold.

# Spec format

A spec is one JSON object. `build_choices.py` validates it and refuses to build from a
bad one, naming every problem it finds.

## Top level

| Key | Required | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `title` | yes | string | States what deciding this set settles. Also the localStorage key. |
| `intro` | no | string | One line of context above the first question. |
| `questions` | yes | list | At least one. |

## Every question

| Key | Required | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | yes | string | Unique. Answers are keyed by it. |
| `type` | yes | string | `choice`, `either`, `text`, `prune`, or `approve`. |
| `q` | yes | string | The question itself. |
| `help` | no | string | Detail shown under the question. |

Unknown keys are rejected rather than ignored, so a `reccommended` typo fails loudly.

## choice

Pick exactly one of N. Renders as a vertical list of cards.

| Key | Required | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `options` | yes | list | Two or more. |
| `options[].label` | yes | string | |
| `options[].detail` | no | string | The consequence of picking it. |
| `options[].recommended` | no | bool | At most one per question. Tags it; does not preselect. |

## either

A binary call. Renders as two large panels, side by side on desktop and stacked on
mobile. Use it when there really are two answers; do not force a third into it.

| Key | Required | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `a` | yes | object | `{label, detail?}` |
| `b` | yes | object | `{label, detail?}` |
| `recommend` | no | string | Exactly `"a"` or `"b"`. |

## text

Free text. Use it only when the answer space genuinely cannot be enumerated. If it can,
research the options and use `choice` instead.

| Key | Required | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `placeholder` | yes | string | One concrete example of a valid answer. |
| `unit` | conditional | string | Required when the question asks for a quantity. |
| `multiline` | no | bool | Enter inserts a newline instead of advancing. |
| `optional` | no | bool | Default false. A required text question blocks the finish state. |

`placeholder` is required because writing one valid answer is the cheapest proof the
question is answerable. An author who cannot write one has not settled what they are
asking.

`unit` becomes required when `q` or `help` contains quantity language: ceiling, budget,
cap, limit, threshold, quota, how much, how many, how often, how long, rate, volume,
spend, amount, price, cost, maximum, minimum, target. Write it as a full phrase, for
example `US dollars per month` or `emails per day`.

## Rejected prose

The builder refuses to build when `q`, `help`, `placeholder`, or any option label or
detail contains hedging. An escape hatch offered to the reader means the question is not
settled.

Rejected: leave blank, or blank, blank if, decide later, if you would rather, if you
prefer, or we can, let me know if, up to you, whatever you, or something, or similar, not
sure, unclear, tbd, ballpark, roughly what.

A `q` containing more than one question mark is also refused. Split it.

### The question this came from

Shipped to the owner on 2026-08-20 and returned unanswered:

```json
{"id": "ceiling", "type": "text",
 "q": "What monthly ceiling do you approve for outreach tooling?",
 "help": "Leave this blank if you would rather see specific vendors and prices first.",
 "placeholder": "a number, or blank to decide later"}
```

He replied: "ceiling for what? spend, volume, different mcps?" The help text gave it away
before he did. The builder now catches this six times over: three hedges, two more in the
placeholder, and a quantity word with no unit. The correct move was to price the vendors
first and offer a `choice`.

## approve

A list where ticking a row is an AFFIRMATIVE YES. Nothing is ticked at load, so
nothing is agreed to by default: an unticked row is withheld, not accepted. This is
the required type for any stamping or ratification list, such as constance OC- token
ceremonies, where prune's keep-by-default reading would count silence as consent.

| Key | Required | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `items` | yes | list | One or more. |
| `items[].label` | yes | string | States what ticking the row settles; for a stamp ceremony, carry the OC- token and rule id. |
| `items[].detail` | no | string | What a tick agrees to, in plain words. |

No suggest flag exists on approve items. A nudge toward yes is not an affirmative yes.

Payload keys are `approved` (ticked) and `withheld` (unticked):

```json
{"id":"stamp","type":"approve","q":"...","approved":["OC-AAA · R001"],"withheld":["OC-BBB · R002"]}
```

Zero ticked is a valid answer and means approve nothing.

## prune

A list where ticking a row marks it FOR DELETION. Nothing is ticked at load.

| Key | Required | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `items` | yes | list | One or more. |
| `items[].label` | yes | string | |
| `items[].detail` | no | string | Why it exists, or what deleting costs. |
| `items[].suggest_delete` | no | bool | Adds a quiet tag. Never pre-ticks. |

Zero ticked is a valid answer and means keep everything.

## The free text box is automatic

Every `choice`, `either`, `prune`, and `approve` question renders a free text box under its options.
There is no spec key for it and no way to switch it off. A `text` question does not get
one, because it already is a free text box.

On `choice` and `either` it is labelled **Something else**. Typing in it answers the
question and deselects any option card, so a listed option is never the only way through.
Free text alone satisfies a required question.

On `prune` and `approve` it is labelled **Anything to add** and is a note only. It never
changes the tick list.

This does not license a vague question. The options still carry real answers with their
consequences, and the recommended option is still marked. The box exists because the
author cannot know every answer, not so the author can stop enumerating the ones he knows.

Never write your own "Other" or "Something else" option into `options` or `items`. It
would sit next to the real one and split the answer.

## Worked example

```json
{
  "title": "Outreach decisions",
  "intro": "Four calls, about two minutes.",
  "questions": [
    {
      "id": "verify",
      "type": "choice",
      "q": "How should the prospect list get cleaned?",
      "help": "The bounce rate is above the level that pauses a channel.",
      "options": [
        {"label": "Approve a verification vendor",
         "detail": "Costs money. Cuts bounces before send and unblocks a higher send rate.",
         "recommended": true},
        {"label": "Hand check the worst lane only",
         "detail": "Free. Slow, and it only fixes one lane."},
        {"label": "Leave it",
         "detail": "The paused lanes stay paused."}
      ]
    },
    {
      "id": "meet",
      "type": "either",
      "q": "Which meeting tool should booking use?",
      "a": {"label": "Google Meet", "detail": "Works over the API today. No sign in needed."},
      "b": {"label": "Zoom", "detail": "Needs a sign in only you can do."},
      "recommend": "a"
    },
    {
      "id": "budget",
      "type": "text",
      "q": "Monthly ceiling for outreach tooling?",
      "placeholder": "for example 150",
      "optional": true
    },
    {
      "id": "lanes",
      "type": "prune",
      "q": "Tick any campaign to retire.",
      "help": "Nothing is ticked. Ticking marks it for deletion.",
      "items": [
        {"label": "a2pagency", "detail": "2 sent, 6 left, paused since 14 Aug", "suggest_delete": true},
        {"label": "requote", "detail": "7 sent, pool empty, 2 replies"},
        {"label": "trades", "detail": "13 sent, live"}
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

## Answer payload

The copy button returns a human summary followed by this JSON:

```json
{"title":"Outreach decisions","answers":[
  {"id":"verify","type":"choice","q":"...","answer":"Approve a verification vendor"},
  {"id":"meet","type":"either","q":"...","answer":"Google Meet"},
  {"id":"budget","type":"text","q":"...","answer":"150"},
  {"id":"lanes","type":"prune","q":"...","delete":["a2pagency"],"keep":["requote","trades"]}
]}
```

`prune` carries both arrays, so a reader acting on `delete` never has to infer `keep`.

### The `other` key

`other` is a string and appears only when the owner typed in the free text box.

On `choice` and `either` its presence means he wrote his own answer rather than picking a
listed option, and `answer` holds that same text. Read `answer` and you are always
correct; read `other` when you need to know he went off the list.

On `prune` it is a note that sits beside `delete` and `keep`.

```json
{"title":"Outreach decisions","answers":[
  {"id":"verify","type":"choice","q":"...","answer":"Ask the vendor for a sample first","other":"Ask the vendor for a sample first"},
  {"id":"lanes","type":"prune","q":"...","delete":["a2pagency"],"keep":["requote","trades"],"other":"also retire the 2024 list"}
]}
```

changes.before: | `title` | yes | string | Names the decision set. Also the localStorage key. |
changes.after: | `title` | yes | string | States what deciding this set settles. Also the localStorage key. |
changes.why: The title instruction asked for a subject name; it now asks the title to state what deciding the set settles.

changes.before: | `items[].label` | yes | string | Carries the thing being approved; for a stamp ceremony, the OC- token and rule id. |
changes.after: | `items[].label` | yes | string | States what ticking the row settles; for a stamp ceremony, carry the OC- token and rule id. |
changes.why: The label instruction asked only that the row carry a subject; it now asks the label to state what ticking settles, keeping the OC- token and rule id as content.

  CTA should go, about section order, hero structure, conversion structure, a CRO audit, or

# Conversion layout

<Reader: a model. The source called its structure "the best converting structure in this
library". No conversion measurement was recovered with it. Present every layout choice here
as a method, never as a measured lift.>

## Scope

Input: the page type, the page's one primary conversion action (estimate request, call,
booking), the project's existing structure or design system if any, and the proof assets
available (reviews, stats, owner presence, work photos, process, map).

Output: a section plan naming each section's job and which conversion surface it points at,
plus an inspection note. The plan is read by the site owner or the implementer: write it
`/simple`; <reader: site owner or the person building the page>.

Out of scope: copy text, keyword placement, form and lead-magnet implementation, colors
and component code (the project owns those), publishing.

## Method

1. **Name the one primary conversion.** One action for the page. Every call to action on
   the page points at that action; placement varies, the offer does not. Competing offers
   ("call us" vs "download" vs "book" vs "chat") split intent. A page can have many
   buttons and one conversion.
2. **Re-offer it at re-engagement points.** The primary capture surface sits where the
   visitor can act without scrolling (source: a form in the hero). Anchor CTAs after the
   human-trust section, after reviews, and in the FAQ link back to the same surface. The
   final section is one clean ask with no new information.
3. **Allow at most one supporting offer.** One lead magnet or tool in one resources band,
   the single place a different capture mechanism appears. Zero is acceptable; two is
   flagged.
4. **Sequence the proof to earn the action.** Everything between the first capture and the
   final ask exists to justify the action. The recovered order of jobs: promise plus proof
   plus capture; quantified credibility; the visitor's problem; the solution; a human
   (owner) presence; social proof; work proof; scope; process; interactive engagement;
   local relevance; objections; local trust; final ask. Keep relative order for the jobs the
   page uses; skip the rest. Use the project's own section order when it has one; this
   sequence is the default, not an override.
5. **Separate layout from implementation.** This skill decides placement and frequency. The
   form, the magnet and the components are built by the project's own means. Do not
   restate their internals here.
6. **Inspect at mobile and desktop.** Confirm: the primary capture is reachable without
   scrolling on desktop and reachable from the hero CTA on mobile (the source used a modal
   there); one supporting offer at most; the final ask is last; the section order matches
   the plan. Use whatever rendering the run provides; if none, report "not inspected".
7. **Report.** Findings in priority order: primary capture missing or hidden first, then
   competing offers, then order breaks, then the rest. State plainly that no conversion
   effect has been measured unless the project has measurements.

## Audit checks

- Primary capture visible without scrolling (desktop) and reachable from the hero (mobile)
- Every CTA points at the same conversion
- Supporting offers: 0 or 1
- Final section is a single ask with no new information
- A human-trust presence (owner or team) exists before the final ask
- Section jobs follow the plan; none reordered by accident

## Gotchas

- A recipe is not a rule. The OVO recipe in `references/ovo-recipe.md` fixes a 14-section
  order, a 7/5 hero grid with a form column, navy concentric-ring closing CTA, and tone
  cycling. Apply it only when the project chooses it; never impose its colors, order or
  hero form on another business.
- The source declared itself the winner over other layout skills. That authority is not
  carried; the project's chosen structure wins here.
- Card grids inside a narrow column collapse; reflow them to full-width rows below their
  minimum width (source line 131).
- Visual breadcrumb navs hide behind sticky headers and break hero centering; the source
  used JSON-LD breadcrumbs instead (line 132).

## References

- `references/ovo-recipe.md`: the OVO-specific structure as a named optional recipe.

## Owner design rule

Do not use eyebrow headings: decorative overlines, small uppercase kickers, or duplicate labels above a main heading. When a heading helps the reader, write one that states what its section concludes; cover the body, read the heading, and write what the section must claim — a different or opposite reading fails. Preserve useful field labels, navigation, and honest task status; they are not decorative headings. Carry this rule into new or revised visual-design guidance.

name: design-exploration
description: Produce meaningfully different visual concepts for one screen or flow, compare them side by side, collect specific feedback, and retain the chosen direction. Use when the user wants to see options, says "show me what this could look like", or dislikes how a screen looks and wants real alternatives instead of adjectives. Not for establishing a product-wide design system (design-system), specifying interaction behavior (interaction-design), or judging an implemented page (design-review).
user-invocable: true
---

# Design exploration

When a screen's look is unresolved, show real alternatives. Visual brainstorming, not a
review process. Derived from GStack `design-shotgun` (MIT, commit
0530392821c277b95e5cd65aa9d9fda4248718b2); see LICENSE in this bundle. The mandatory
different-font/font-palette/layout ban, numerical taste scores, and endless regeneration
loops were deliberately not carried over.

## Brief before generating

Establish five things, reusing what already exists (the product's design system file,
existing components, the flow the user described):

1. **Who** the screen is for and their expertise level.
2. **Job** — what the user is trying to accomplish on this screen.
3. **What exists** — components and patterns already available.
4. **Flow** — how users arrive and where they go next.
5. **Edge cases** — long content, zero results, errors, mobile, first-time versus
   experienced users.

Resolve the consequential gaps and proceed with clearly stated routine assumptions; preserve the owner's chosen depth of planning. If the
complaint is about an existing screen, evolve from that actual screen rather than starting
from nothing.

## Generate genuinely distinct directions

Give each concept a distinct one-line direction, then render the requested options using the settled brief:

```
A) "Name stating what the concept claims" — one-line visual description
B) "Name stating what the concept claims" — one-line visual description
C) "Name stating what the concept claims" — one-line visual description
```

Distinctness is the requirement. Each variant must differ in what it *communicates* —
visual temperature, density, hierarchy, personality — not merely shuffle decorative
values. Compare the rendered options and name their visible differences in hierarchy, structure or character; the same realistic content can appear in genuinely different concepts. Two or three variants are usually enough; more only
when the brief genuinely supports it.

Variation must fit the brief and the established brand. If a design system exists, it is
the default constraint; depart from it only when the user asks, and name the departure.
Never change the brand's typeface or palette just to manufacture difference — vary
layout, hierarchy, density, imagery, and expressive treatment instead.

## Render, compare, retain

- Render each concept with realistic content and look at the actual result at mobile and
  desktop widths. Generation alone proves nothing about appearance.
- Present all variants together, side by side, so the comparison happens between real
  images rather than descriptions. Report any variant that failed to render instead of
  silently skipping it.
- Collect specific feedback: which variant, what works, what does not, in the user's
  words. State your interpretation briefly and apply clear feedback; ask only when a consequential ambiguity remains.
- Refine the preferred direction using that feedback, or regenerate one variant in a
  deliberately different direction when nothing on the board is right. Stop when the user
  has a direction they chose; do not keep generating to chase a score.
- Retain the decision: save the chosen concept, the runner-up, and the feedback with the
  project's design material, so the next session reuses this decision instead of redoing
  the exploration.

If the product-wide direction is what is missing rather than this one screen, hand off to
`nautilus-core:design-system` first.

Fable 5.1 owns design, layout, interaction quality and direct refinement through the configured Nautilus route. Supply the settled brief and references; if that route is unavailable, report the specific gap and continue independent work. Do not silently substitute a model.

No eyebrow headings, decorative overlines, small uppercase kickers, or duplicate labels above the main heading. Preserve useful field labels, navigation and honest task status.

# Design language transfer

Translate an observed visual system into the project's existing design primitives while preserving content, behavior, and project structure.

## Boundaries

- Capture publicly observable visual properties and implementation signals. Do not copy text, logos, illustrations, proprietary assets, or application behavior.
- Keep section order and conversion placement unchanged unless the user has authorized structural changes. Use `conversion-layout` when its methods help with that authorized work.
- Use only capture tools available in the current run. If Bright Data is explicitly required, use the native `brightdata-collection` Chart for that collection step; do not use the archived shell scripts or handle credentials here.
- The source entered Git on 2026-05-12. That proves source presence, not production use or current third-party tool behavior.

## Method

1. **Fix the scope.** Name the reference URL or supplied image, target project surface, pages or components to restyle, required states, and properties that must remain unchanged.
2. **Capture evidence.** Gather a rendered desktop view, a mobile view, and HTML/CSS evidence when available. Include interaction states relevant to the requested surface. Follow [capture and extraction](references/capture-and-extraction.md).
3. **Separate observation from inference.** Tag each value as exact CSS, repeated implementation pattern, visual estimate, or unavailable. Never present an estimated color, spacing value, font, or effect as exact.
4. **Build the token map.** Record color roles, typography, spacing, radii, borders, shadows, gradients, motion, breakpoints, and recurring component treatments. Resolve conflicts before editing. Use [the token-map format](references/token-map.md).
5. **Map into the project.** Identify the existing framework, global theme, token layer, component library, and affected components. Prefer adapting existing tokens and theme hooks to scattering literal values.
6. **Apply in layers.** Move from global surfaces and typography to containers, controls, component details, and distinctive effects. Preserve behavior and data flow. Follow [application and visual proof](references/application-and-proof.md).
7. **Render and inspect.** Compare before and after at the declared widths and states. Check layout, contrast, focus, hover, overflow, wrapping, and motion. Then compare the rendered result against the source evidence itself, not only against your own before shots: read computed font, color, spacing, radius, and shadow values from the rendered DOM and check each against the token map's tagged source values, so an implementation drift or an estimate that hardened into a token is caught rather than reproduced. Fix material differences caused by the implementation; list reference details intentionally left out.
8. **Report simply.** Lead with what now matches, what remains approximate, and the files changed. Include the token map or its path and the visual evidence inspected. Human-facing output is `/simple`.

## Related website methods

For scaffold-derived website work, use [website design methods](references/website-design-methods.md) when diagnosing hero hydration, gallery duplication, section containers, token roles, or overlay layers. Historical brand and layout values are examples; preserve the current project’s design brief.

## Stop conditions

Infer the target and scope from the task and project when clear. Ask only when a missing target or conflicting preservation boundary prevents the requested edit. If capture evidence is incomplete, produce a bounded token hypothesis and label it; do not invent exact values. If the requested change would alter conversion structure, route that part to `conversion-layout` instead of folding it into this Chart.

## Owner design rule

Do not use eyebrow headings: decorative overlines, small uppercase kickers, or duplicate labels above a main heading. When a heading helps the reader, write one that states what its section concludes; cover the body, read the heading, and write what the section must claim — a different or opposite reading fails. Preserve useful field labels, navigation, and honest task status; they are not decorative headings. Carry this rule into new or revised visual-design guidance.

Load when writing the corresponding document type. Adapt headings to the project's existing
conventions; keep the content contract. The delivered headings state what their sections conclude rather than repeating these template names.

## Reference

````markdown
# [Entity Name]

[One paragraph: what it is, what it does, when to use it.]

## Interface

[Complete public surface: functions, commands, options, parameters.
Types, defaults, and constraints pulled directly from code.]

## Configuration

[Every option: type, default, effect.]

## Examples

[2-3 examples that run when copy-pasted.]

## Related

[Links to the how-to and explanation docs for this entity.]
````

## Explanation

````markdown
# [Concept or decision]

[The problem this design solves, in terms a reader who has not seen the code understands.]

## The problem

[Concrete failure mode without this design — real, not hypothetical.]

## The approach

[How the design solves it. A small ASCII diagram is fine: grep-able and diff-friendly.]

## Trade-offs

[What was given up. "We chose X over Y because Z."]

## Alternatives considered

[What was tried or rejected and why, if discoverable from history or ADRs.]
````

## How-to

````markdown
# How to [accomplish the task]

[What the reader accomplishes and the end result.]

## Prerequisites

[Versions, tools, config state — specific.]

## Steps

1. [Action verb] [specific instruction]

   ```bash
   [exact command]
   ```

   [Expected result when non-obvious.]

## Verification

[Command, URL, or test that confirms it worked.]

## Troubleshooting

[Common failure modes and fixes, drawn from tests and error handling.]
````

````markdown
# [What the reader will build or learn]

[Concrete: "You will build a working X that does Y."]

[Prerequisites, linked to installation guidance.]

[Show every command; explain briefly on first encounter.]

[Something visibly works by step 3. If not, restructure.]

[What the reader now has, what it can do, and where to go next.]
````

# ADR Format

ADRs live in `docs/adr/` and use sequential numbering: `0001-slug.md`, `0002-slug.md`, etc.

Create the `docs/adr/` directory lazily: only when the first ADR is needed.

## Template

```md
# {Title stating what the decision settles}

{1-3 sentences: what's the context, what did we decide, and why.}
```

That's it. An ADR can be a single paragraph. The value is in recording *that* a decision was made and *why*: not in filling out sections. The title states what the decision settles; cover the body, read the title, and a different or opposite reading fails.

## Optional sections

Only include these when they add genuine value. Most ADRs won't need them.

- **Status** frontmatter (`proposed | accepted | deprecated | superseded by ADR-NNNN`): useful when decisions are revisited
- **Considered Options**: only when the rejected alternatives are worth remembering
- **Consequences**: only when non-obvious downstream effects need to be called out

## Numbering

Scan `docs/adr/` for the highest existing number and increment by one.

## When to offer an ADR

All three of these must be true:

1. **Hard to reverse**: the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context**: a future reader will look at the code and wonder "why on earth did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off**: there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If a decision is easy to reverse, skip it: you'll just reverse it. If it's not surprising, nobody will wonder why. If there was no real alternative, there's nothing to record beyond "we did the obvious thing."

### What qualifies

- **Architectural shape.** "We're using a monorepo." "The write model is event-sourced, the read model is projected into Postgres."
- **Integration patterns between contexts.** "Ordering and Billing communicate via domain events, not synchronous HTTP."
- **Technology choices that carry lock-in.** Database, message bus, auth provider, deployment target. Not every library: just the ones that would take a quarter to swap out.
- **Boundary and scope decisions.** "Customer data is owned by the Customer context; other contexts reference it by ID only." The explicit no-s are as valuable as the yes-s.
- **Deliberate deviations from the obvious path.** "We're using manual SQL instead of an ORM because X." Anything where a reasonable reader would assume the opposite. These stop the next engineer from "fixing" something that was deliberate.
- **Constraints not visible in the code.** "We can't use AWS because of compliance requirements." "Response times must be under 200ms because of the partner API contract."
- **Rejected alternatives when the rejection is non-obvious.** If you considered GraphQL and picked REST for subtle reasons, record it: otherwise someone will suggest GraphQL again in six months.

# Explainer

Create one polished, standalone HTML page that explains `$ARGUMENTS`. This Chart grants no
authority and enforces nothing by itself: the current task, the user's direction, and runtime
enforcement govern every action, and a user correction outranks any earlier text in this file.

## When to reach for it

Beyond a direct request, prefer a page over plaintext when a visual reference cuts ambiguity:
architecture maps, operating-model or cockpit concepts, before/after redesign directions,
workflow or agent-lane diagrams, dashboard mockups, decision trees, compliance or process cheat
sheets. Do not replace a direct answer with HTML for a simple question; the page must clarify a
decision, not become decorative overhead. The reply still states the answer plainly.

If the subject is a manual provider-console flow (carrier registration, OAuth consent, portal
handoffs), read [references/compliance-cheat-sheet-pattern.md](references/compliance-cheat-sheet-pattern.md)
and build to it. Its save-location line is superseded by "Save location" below.

## Readers and registers

This file and the checker output are read by a model and follow
[../precise/SKILL.md](../precise/SKILL.md). The page is read by a human:
<simple: the page, written for one reader who has never seen the project, in concept: what
happened and why it matters to them>. Owner ruling 2026-09-03: simple is the norm for anything
a human reads; a technical page is the exception and requires the requester to ask for it in
that request.

Voice, every sentence of the page (owner ruling 2026-09-03 23:44):

- The output never names the owner and never refers to him in the third person. Address the
  reader as "you". Where a third party may read it and the role matters, write "the owner".
- No praise, thanks, or deference toward the owner or the reader. Write so the page could be
  published as a plain description of what the system did.
- A register direction is an instruction to the writer, never a sentence in the output. In
  skill text, wrap every register direction in angle brackets.

## Writing

Read [../simple/SKILL.md](../simple/SKILL.md) before writing a word of the page and apply it
to every headline, heading, and caption. Ablated 2026-08-14: without the clarity rules this
skill produced reversal headlines in 2 of 2 runs and scored 4 of 10 against 9.5 with them.

- **Reader model.** One reader who has never seen the project, the tools, or the vocabulary,
  and who knows how a workplace runs: managers, rules, inspectors, doors, switches. Introduce
  every technical object as one of those before its real name, if its real name appears at all.
- **Sentences.** One idea each, 12 to 20 words, no semicolons. Never build a title or heading
  on a turn ("Not X, but Y"; "It wasn't A. It was B."). Cut any line that carries no fact.
- **Numbers.** Each number appears once with its unit and a source phrase in a caption or table
  cell. Never invent metrics; label sample data as sample.
- **Names.** A technical name appears at most once per page, inside `<code>`, only when the
  reader must open it; elsewhere use the analogy noun. One analogy per concept, held for the
  whole page. Example from the 2026-09-03 reference page: rule = sign on the wall or locked
  door; enforcement = gatekeeper at the door; ignored hook = smoke detector without batteries.
- **Headline.** States what the page concludes in the reader's words, with its headline number.
- **Provider or API architecture docs.** Verify current docs or specs first and label each
  conclusion `documented`, `live verified`, or `not documented`; never "probably" or "likely"
  when the requester asked for doc-backed conclusions.

## Structure

Density floor, every page: at least 2 sections : 1 table : 1 inline `<svg>` diagram. The
checker counts literal `<section`, `<table`, and `<svg` tags; a CSS box is not a diagram.

**Status or report template** (scope: a page that answers "what happened and why it matters";
source: the reference build approved 2026-09-03). Four sections, two-digit numbers, headings
stating what each section concludes, in this order. Cover the body, read the heading, and write what the section must claim; a different or opposite reading fails:

| # | Section answers | Required element |
|---|---|---|
| 01 | Who was involved and what question was asked | one `<svg>`: actors as labeled boxes, arrows for who talks to whom, the object under study below |
| 02 | What was found | one two-kinds analogy, one `<svg>` comparing them with the counts, one table with counts and a one-line plain meaning per row |
| 03 | What was built and why it matters to the reader | a bordered "Result" block stating the question and its yes/no answer; an `<h3>` stating why the result matters to the reader |
| 04 | What happened to the work and what the owner decides next | a table of pending decisions: number, a name stating what deciding it settles, one plain sentence; close with the exact file the owner acts on and the verbs for it |

Four sections hold the 2:1:1 floor with two tables and two diagrams. Fold extra material into
03 or 04 as an `<h3>`; do not add a fifth section to this template.

**Size, every other subject.** Default to short. Pick the size before writing; a page that grew
while writing gets cut back to its tier. Length is never the goal.

| Size | Build | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| Short | The density floor and nothing more. One screen of scroll. | Default. |
| Medium | One added section per extra cause or open decision. Add a timeline when order changes the answer. | 2 or more independent causes, or 2 or more open decisions. |
| Long | One section per system, plus one diagram per boundary crossed. | 3 or more systems, or the owner acts across more than one day. |

## Visual treatment

- The polished treatment is the default: strong visual hierarchy with cards, lanes, timelines,
  and inline diagrams, never a text page with headings. Choose the structure and treatment that
  fit the subject. Do not reuse a default palette, page structure, or component set across
  unrelated explainers.
- Status and report explainers (owner-set 2026-08-29): white-background editorial scientific
  treatment: serif body, numbered small-caps sections, captioned figures with sources, hairline
  tables with a heavy top rule, and a working PDF.
- Typography: set the type system first (roles, scale, measure, leading), then apply it to the
  page. Hard floor: no text computes below 16px at any viewport, chrome included.
- If the subject is GSP-OS, treat the output as an operational cockpit, not a decorative
  dashboard.
- Semantic HTML, responsive layout, readable contrast, working internal links. No horizontal
  overflow at 390px or 1440px. Wide tables inside CSS-grid cards: give grid children
  `min-width:0`, or one table's min-width propagates through the grid and overflows the whole
  page (measured 2026-08-25 at both widths).
- Keep all CSS and JavaScript in the file. No network assets, external fonts, CDNs, or runtime
  fetches. The page opens whole from disk with no server behind it; never stand up a preview
  server for it.

## Inline SVG diagrams

Plan the geometry before writing markup: a fixed card grid, every text string width-checked
against its container at the font size used. The 16px floor binds inside diagrams: size type
against the SVG's smallest rendered width, not the viewBox. An SVG wider than the mobile
viewport sits in an `overflow-x` scroll wrapper, the one allowed exception to the no-overflow
rule.

- No line, arrow, or connector passes through text. Draw a line in segments with a real gap
  where its label sits; route the one crossing a boundary line through a cut in that line.
- A line's label sits beside it in open canvas, never on it.
- Text keeps clearance of at least half its own font size from any border it does not belong to.
- Under 760px, set `svg{min-width:<viewBox width>px}` inside the `.scroll` wrapper so labels
  render 1:1 and the figure scrolls sideways; text keeps 8px or more from any box edge. Measured
  2026-09-03: a 240-unit box clipped a 16px label; 300 units cleared it.
- Bound SVG scale in both directions. At each viewport, rendered label size = SVG font size x
  rendered SVG width / viewBox width. Keep the smallest label at least 16px and the largest no
  larger than the page's `h2`; set an explicit desktop `max-width` instead of unbounded
  `width:100%`. Probe both bounds at 390px and 1440px before handover. Measured 2026-08-31: a
  350-unit diagram stretched to 996px turned 16-unit labels into 45.53px text; capping it at
  460px produced 21.03px labels.

Owner-rejected 2026-08-25: lines crossed labels and subtitles touched borders.

## Make PDF button and print

Every page carries one "Make PDF" button, styled to match the page, plus a smaller "Copy agent
prompt" action beside it.

- "Make PDF" calls `window.print()`. Ship `@media print` CSS in the file: hide both controls,
  keep backgrounds and text legible, never break a page inside a card, table, or `<svg>`.
- "Copy agent prompt" writes this line to the clipboard with the page's real absolute save path
  baked in at build time:
  `/make-pdf <abs-path> (standalone explainer HTML: render it to PDF mechanically with the Chromium print engine; never convert it to markdown or rebuild it)`
  The markdown warning is load-bearing: a markdown round trip degrades the page. Whether a
  `/make-pdf` command exists on the host is not established by this Chart; the checker measures
  only the string and its path.

Print standard (owner-set 2026-08-29), every page:

- `@page { size: letter; margin: 0; }`: zero page margins remove the browser's printed filename,
  date, and URL edge stamps. The body carries the real margins as `body{padding:15mm 14mm}`
  inside `@media print`.
- `.scroll{overflow:visible}` and `svg, figure img{max-width:100%; height:auto}` in print, so
  wide figures scale into the page instead of clipping.
- `-webkit-print-color-adjust:exact; print-color-adjust:exact` on everything tinted.
- `figure,.stamp,table,.pull{break-inside:avoid}`, `tr{break-inside:avoid}`, `h2{break-after:avoid}`.

Print verification: if a print engine is available to the harness, emit a real PDF
(recorded test: `page.emulate_media(media="print")` then
`page.pdf(format="Letter", print_background=True, display_header_footer=True)`) and open it;
with `display_header_footer=True`, a page that still shows a filename, date, or URL on the
edge fails. If no print engine is available, report the print output as unverified.

## Save location

If the task names an output path, use it. Otherwise save in the current task's output location.
The filename carries a date stamp (`YYYY-MM-DD`, or `YYYYMMDD-HHMM` for a one-time page); a
dateless deliverable is a defect. Do not overwrite an existing file unless the task asked for
that exact path. Build the page at its final path: the checker compares the `/make-pdf` prompt
against the file's own absolute path.

## Build, check, inspect, loop

**BUILD** produces the complete page.

**CHECK** runs, from this skill's directory:

`python3 scripts/verify_html.py <abs-path>`

Add `--no-browser` when the `browse` CLI is absent (`BROWSE_BIN` unset and not on `PATH`).
The parsing half measures: network fetches (tags, CSS `url()`, `@import`), `href="#id"`
targets, the 2:1:1 floor (`--ratio`), and the three PDF-button signals (`--pdf-button`). The
browser half, only with `browse`, measures at 1440x1100 and 390x850: non-empty `<title>`,
non-zero height, `scrollWidth <= clientWidth + 1`, and writes one full-page screenshot per
width. Exit 0 proves only those measurements. The checker does not measure the 16px floor,
label clearance, line crossings, print rules, sentence length, reversal headings, or any
rendered geometry. Its tests: `python3 scripts/test_verify_html.py` (36 tests, stdlib only).
The checker is a local check; it is not a Watch validator unless the release binds it.

**INSPECT** covers what the checker cannot. Use the harness's available browser or screenshot
tool to view the page at 390px and 1440px, and read the screenshots the checker wrote when the
browser half ran. If headless Chrome `--window-size` is the capture route, confirm the
rendered `clientWidth`: measured 2026-08-25, its window width floored near 500px and rendered a
485px layout labeled 390. If no browser or screenshot tool is available, open the page for
the requester through the host UI and report that the agent's visual inspection did not run.
Then answer three questions: (1) is any sentence understandable only with project context;
(2) does any heading turn on a reversal; (3) is the smallest diagram label 16px or more at
390px. Fix each before handover. The 2026-09-03 draft failed (2) with "signs, not locks" and
(3) with 8px labels.

**LOOP** fixes observed defects and repeats the affected checks. Once checks and inspection
pass, deliver; do not repeat them without a new change or unresolved concern. Report unavailable
checks plainly; never treat them as a pass. Respect permission denials. An available alternative
tool may complete the authorized check without bypassing the denied boundary.

**HANDOVER.** Open the finished file through the host UI when one is available (`open
<abs-path>` on macOS). Reply <simple: the absolute path, the one decision the page unblocks,
what the checker measured, and what was not measured or inspected>.

## Outside this Chart

The current task and platform instructions define authorization. This Chart adds no purchase,
publishing, or approval authority and no standing review step. Use an already authorized route;
request only genuinely missing authority.

name: handoff
description: Compact the current conversation into a handoff document for another agent to pick up.
argument-hint: "What will the next session be used for?"
disable-model-invocation: true
---

Write a handoff document summarising the current conversation so a fresh agent can continue the work.

**Destination.** Save the document to durable task state that outlives this session: the existing task workspace or state directory the work already uses. Do not default to OS temporary storage; a handoff lost to a temp cleanup is not a handoff. If the owner names a temporary destination for this handoff, write exactly there and say in the reply that it is temporary. Record the document's absolute path in the reply.

Include these sections; the handoff's own headings state what each section claims rather than repeating these list names:

- **Suggested skills**: the skills the next session should invoke for this work, by name.
- **Current state pointers**: active run/attempt identifiers, checker or validation commands with their last recorded result, accepted or in-flight artifact paths and revisions, recorded effects and their receipts, and the recovery route if the next session is interrupted.
- **Requirements and completion boundary**: point to the existing requirement record by its durable path so the next session loads it before choosing work rather than starting a competing ledger; preserve every unfinished requirement, user correction, explicit cancellation, delivery boundary, and evidence gap. Distinguish staged, accepted, integrated, and active results. Do not turn a handoff into completion or drop a requirement because the topic changed.
- **Next ready work**: the specific items whose dependencies are now satisfied, and the exact question, recommendation, and affected work for anything blocked on a decision.

Do not duplicate content already captured in other artifacts (specs, plans, ADRs, issues, commits, diffs). Reference them by path or URL instead. Do not resurrect a completed launch or approval step: reuse settled decisions and existing approval; name only decisions that are genuinely still open.

Redact any sensitive information, such as API keys, passwords, or personally identifiable information.

If the user passed arguments, treat them as a description of what the next session will focus on and tailor the doc accordingly.

<simple: the findings, recommendations and deliverable prose read by the user.>

# HTML Report Format The architectural review is rendered as a single self-contained HTML file in the OS temp directory. Tailwind and Mermaid both come from CDNs. Mermaid handles graph-shaped diagrams reliably; hand-built divs and inline SVG handle the more editorial visuals (mass diagrams, cross-sections). Mix the two: don't lean on Mermaid for everything, it'll start to look generic. ## Scaffold ```html Architecture review: {{repo name}}
...
...
...
``` ## Header Repo name, date, and a compact legend: solid box = module, dashed line = seam, red arrow = leakage, thick dark box = deep module. No introduction paragraph: straight into the candidates. ## Candidate card The diagrams carry the weight. Prose is sparse, plain, and uses the glossary terms (from the `/codebase-design` skill) without ceremony. Each candidate is one `
`: - **Title**: a clause stating what the deepening settles (e.g. "Collapse the Order intake pipeline"). - **Badge row**: recommendation strength (`Strong` = emerald, `Worth exploring` = amber, `Speculative` = slate), plus a tag for the dependency category (`in-process`, `local-substitutable`, `ports & adapters`, `mock`). - **Files**: monospaced list, `font-mono text-sm`. - **Before / After diagram**: the centrepiece. Two columns, side by side. See patterns below. - **Problem**: one sentence. What hurts. - **Solution**: one sentence. What changes. - **Wins**: bullets, ≤6 words each. e.g. "Tests hit one interface", "Pricing logic stops leaking", "Delete 4 shallow wrappers". - **ADR callout** (if applicable): one line in an amber-tinted box. No paragraphs of explanation. If the diagram needs a paragraph to be understood, redraw the diagram. ## Diagram patterns Pick the pattern that fits the candidate. Mix them. Don't make every diagram look the same: variety is part of the point. ### Mermaid graph (the workhorse for dependencies / call flow) Use a Mermaid `flowchart` or `graph` when the point is "X calls Y calls Z, and look at the mess." Wrap it in a Tailwind-styled card so it doesn't feel parachuted in. Style with classDef to colour leakage edges red and the deep module dark. Sequence diagrams work well for "before: 6 round-trips; after: 1." ```html 
    flowchart LR
      A[OrderHandler] --> B[OrderValidator]
      B --> C[OrderRepo]
      C -.leak.-> D[PricingClient]
      classDef leak stroke:#dc2626,stroke-width:2px;
      class C,D leak
``` ### Hand-built boxes-and-arrows (when Mermaid's layout fights you) Modules as `
`s with borders and labels. Arrows as inline SVG `` or `` elements positioned absolutely over a relative container. Reach for this when you want the "after" diagram to feel like one thick-bordered deep module with greyed-out internals: Mermaid won't render that with the right weight. ### Cross-section (good for layered shallowness) Stack horizontal bands (`h-12 border-l-4`) to show layers a call passes through. Before: 6 thin layers each doing nothing. After: 1 thick band labelled with the consolidated responsibility. ### Mass diagram (good for "interface as wide as implementation") Two rectangles per module: one for interface surface area, one for implementation. Before: interface rectangle is nearly as tall as the implementation rectangle (shallow). After: interface rectangle is short, implementation rectangle is tall (deep). ### Call-graph collapse Before: a tree of function calls rendered as nested boxes. After: the same tree collapsed into one box, with the now-internal calls shown faded inside it. ## Style guidance - Lean editorial, not corporate-dashboard. Generous whitespace. Serif optional for headings (`font-serif` works well with stone/slate). - Colour sparingly: one accent (emerald or indigo) plus red for leakage and amber for warnings. - Keep diagrams ~320px tall so before/after sits comfortably side by side without scrolling. - Use `text-xs uppercase tracking-wider` for module labels inside diagrams: they should read as schematic, not as UI. - The only scripts are the Tailwind CDN and the Mermaid ESM import. The report is otherwise static: no app code, no interactivity beyond Mermaid's own rendering. ## Top recommendation section One larger card. Candidate name, one sentence on why, anchor link to its card. That's it. ## Tone Plain English, concise, but the architectural nouns and verbs come straight from the `/codebase-design` skill. Concision is not an excuse to drift. **Use exactly:** module, interface, implementation, depth, deep, shallow, seam, adapter, leverage, locality. **Never substitute:** component, service, unit (for module) · API, signature (for interface) · boundary (for seam) · layer, wrapper (for module, when you mean module). **Phrasings that fit the style:** - "Order intake module is shallow: interface nearly matches the implementation." - "Pricing leaks across the seam." - "Deepen: one interface, one place to test." - "Two adapters justify the seam: HTTP in prod, in-memory in tests." **Wins bullets** name the gain in glossary terms: *"locality: bugs concentrate in one module"*, *"leverage: one interface, N call sites"*, *"interface shrinks; implementation absorbs the wrappers"*. Don't write *"easier to maintain"* or *"cleaner code"*: those terms aren't in the glossary and don't earn their place. No hedging, no throat-clearing, no "it's worth noting that…". If a sentence could be a bullet, make it a bullet. If a bullet could be cut, cut it. If a term isn't in the `/codebase-design` glossary, reach for one that is before inventing a new one.
